power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .064", "p = .064"), Sentence = c("Indirect interaction studies showed a larger but statistically nonsignificant and less precise effect size estimate, d = 0.0006, 95% CI [-0.00001-0.0012], p = .064; I² = 25.2%).", "Direct-intention studies showed a statistically significant mean effect size (d = 0.0017, p = .04), whereas indirect or field-based studies showed a larger nominal effect estimate (d = 0.0006) but with lower precision and no conventional statistical significance (p = .064)." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

text.text: This updated meta-analysis evaluated evidence for direct and indirect mental interactions with random binary event generators (RNGs) in studies published after the meta-analysis by Bösch, Steinkamp, and Boller (2006).
text.formatted: This updated meta-analysis evaluated evidence for direct and indirect mental interactions with random binary event generators (RNGs) in studies published after the meta-analysis by <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Bösch, Steinkamp, and Boller (2006)</ref>.

text.text: The aim was to estimate the overall magnitude and precision of reported effects, assess between-study heterogeneity and potential publication bias, and compare findings across direct intention and indirect field-based protocols.
Studies were identified through database searches, specialist journals and conference proceedings, an AI-assisted literature search, and contact with researchers in the field.

Forty-nine eligible studies were included: 18 direct-interaction studies, in which participants intentionally attempted to influence RNG outputs, and 28 indirect-interaction studies, in which RNG activity was examined in relation to collective human attention.
Direct interaction studies showed a small positive overall per trial effect size d = 0.0017, 95% CI [0.0001, 0.0033], p = .041; I² = 0%.
Indirect interaction studies showed a larger but statistically nonsignificant and less precise effect size estimate, d = 0.0006, 95% CI [-0.00001-0.0012], p = .064; I² = 25.2%).
Moderator analyses of direct studies suggested larger effects among selected participants and in bidirectional-intention tasks, although these estimates were imprecise and based on few studies.
Selection-model, excess-significance, and proportion-of-significant-results analyses indicated possible publication bias in both research paradigms.
Overall, the findings suggest small deviations from chance in direct RNG-interaction studies, whereas evidence for indirect effects remains uncertain because of lower precision.
Potential selective reporting and the limited number of studies constrain firm conclusions, highlighting the need for preregistered, adequately powered, and independently replicated investigations.

Whether human mental states can exert a systematic, statistically detectable influence on the behavior of certified physical random systems is one of the most empirically demanding questions in anomalous cognition research.

The experimental program addressing this question spans more than six decades, involves hundreds of laboratories across multiple continents, and has generated a literature of several thousand published reports.
Yet, no consensus has emerged, not because the data are sparse, but because the data are deeply contested along methodological, statistical, and theoretical lines that resist easy resolution.

The present meta-analysis enters this debate with the specific aim of providing the most comprehensive and methodologically transparent quantitative synthesis to date, covering both direct protocols in which individuals or groups consciously attempt to bias an RNG output, and "field" (indirect) protocols in which distributed RNG networks are monitored for coherence anomalies during periods of large-scale collective human attention, encompassing both localized non-intentional/implicit group or healing settings (FieldREG) and global collective attention events (GCP).
The use of electronic random number generators as targets for putative mind-matter interactions (MMI) emerged from the earlier dice-throwing tradition.

Helmut Schmidt's mid-20th-century work, conducted with apparatus based on quantum-level radioactive decay and electronic noise sources, established the foundational design logic: if a device whose outputs are determined by processes that are, in principle, immune to classical perturbation shows systematic deviations correlated with the stated intention of a human participant, conventional explanations must be excluded before an anomalous conclusion can be entertained.

Schmidt's early electronic PK studies (Schmidt, 1970; 2017) remain among the most frequently cited primary sources in this literature, with the apparatus design using a quantum noise source driving a binary display setting the template adopted by nearly all subsequent direct interaction researchers.

text.text: The paradigm was institutionalized and scaled through the Princeton Engineering Anomalies Research (PEAR) laboratory, where Robert Jahn and Brenda Dunne (Dunne & Jahn, 1995) conducted what would become the benchmark dataset: a twelve-year program involving 91 volunteer participants generating approximately 2.5 million RNG trials, within which HI (intend-high) and LO (intend-low) conditions were compared against a baseline (BL) control.

Bancel and Nelson (2008), reporting on 236 world events accumulated over nine years of continuous operation, found that "the cumulative significance across all events favors the hypothesis by more than 4.5 standard deviations," with secondary analyses suggesting the result is driven by correlations across global RNG network distances, an architecturally non-trivial finding that distinguishes genuine network coherence from simple univariate deviation.

text.text: By the formal experiment's completion across 500 pre-specified events covering the period 1998-2015, Nelson (2024) reports that the accumulated departure exceeds 7 standard deviations.

Because the GCP constitutes a single continuously running experiment rather than a series of independent replications, the critical assessment focuses less on study-to-study consistency and more on analytical validity within that single protocol, event selection operationalization, temporal window specification, post-hoc secondary analyses, and the adequacy of pre-specification, given that events are identified from news reports after the fact.
The theoretical interpretation for both paradigm families is underdeveloped relative to the accumulated data.

Direct micro-PK accounts range from decision augmentation theory (May, Utts, & Spottiswoode, 1995), which locates the anomaly in precognitive information use at decision points rather than physical biasing, to von Lucadou's Correlation Matrix Method model (von Lucadou, Römer, & Walach, 2007), which frames psi effects as non-local correlations governed by organizational closure constraints to quantum-measurement observer-collapse models that attribute RNG deviations to the act of conscious observation (Maier, Dechamps and Rabeyron, 2022; Radin and Cline, 2026).

text.text: None of these frameworks has achieved sufficient specificity to generate differential predictions that could adjudicate between competing accounts using the existing data.

For the field paradigm, the dominant theoretical commitment is to some form of "consciousness field", the hypothesis that largescale coherence of human attention constitutes a physically detectable state that correlates with anomalous structure in physically distributed random systems.

Holmberg's (2026) Cognitive Entropy Shift Model, which suggests that distinct cognitive states modulate probabilistic systems by reducing entropy, represents a more recent theoretical candidate, although its empirical status is preliminary.
The present meta-analysis is an update from the Bösch, Steinkamp, and Boller (2006) metaanalysis through 2026 for direct and indirect interaction experimental protocols.
Effect sizes are expressed as per-trial standardized effect sizes (denoted as d) to permit cross-paradigm comparison. .
The goal is not to adjudicate the ontological claim of whether mind-matter interaction in the sense of anomalous RNG biasing exists as a genuine physical phenomenon.

The meta-analysis can determine what the current experimental database, taken as a whole and evaluated by contemporary standards of methodological transparency, does and does not support and what experimental designs would be required to generate stronger evidence in either direction.

This updated meta-analysis synthesized post-2004 studies examining direct and indirect mental interaction with random number generators (RNGs).
Overall, the findings indicate small positive pooled effects for both paradigms.

Direct-intention studies showed a statistically significant mean effect size (d = 0.0017, p = .04), whereas indirect or field-based studies showed a larger nominal effect estimate (d = 0.0006) but with lower precision and no conventional statistical significance (p = .064).

Thus, the evidence provides limited support for deviations from expected RNG behavior associated with human mental activity, but the magnitude of these effects is extremely small and their interpretation remains uncertain.
The direct-interaction results are notable because they were associated with very low overall heterogeneity (I² = 0.1%).
This suggests that the included studies produced relatively consistent effectsize estimates despite differences in participants, apparatuses, protocols, and intention instructions.
However, homogeneity alone does not establish the validity of an anomalous effect, particularly given the indications of publication bias.
The selection-model effect size estimates were non-significant for both direct and indirect studies, and the PSST and TESS analyses suggested an excess of statistically significant findings.
The direct-interaction studies produced a nominal effect approximately three times larger than that observed in indirect-intention studies.
Nevertheless, this finding should not be interpreted as evidence that field effects are stronger.
The indirect estimate was less precise, and the reported confidence interval indicates substantial uncertainty around the pooled effect.
In addition, indirect studies differ fundamentally from direct studies in their sampling, event definition, temporal structure, data volume, and analytic flexibility.

Field protocols may involve very large numbers of trials and naturally occurring events, but these features also increase the importance of transparent eventselection criteria, preregistration of analysis windows, correction for multiple testing, and clear separation between confirmatory and exploratory analyses.
The moderator analyses provide tentative evidence that selected participants and bidirectional tasks may be associated with larger effects in direct-intention studies.
Selected participants showed an approximately five fold larger mean effect size than unselected participants, and bidirectional intention tasks showed a larger mean effect than unidirectional tasks.
However, neither the selected-participant nor the bidirectional-task subgroup reached conventional statistical significance, and heterogeneity was substantial in these subgroups.
These results should therefore be considered hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory.
They may reflect genuine differences in participant characteristics or task demands, but they could also arise from small study numbers, selective reporting, or differences in experimental quality.
A major strength of this review is its inclusion of both direct and indirect RNG-interaction paradigms.

Most previous quantitative syntheses have focused primarily on direct intentional influence, whereas the present analysis allows a structured comparison between individual intentional protocols and field-based designs.

This broader scope helps clarify that the two paradigms should not be treated as interchangeable: they involve different theoretical assumptions, operational definitions, and methodological vulnerabilities.
A second strength is the use of contemporary random-effects meta-analytic methods, including restricted maximum likelihood estimation and Hartung-type confidence intervals.
These methods are appropriate when effect sizes may vary across studies and provide more conservative uncertainty estimates than simpler fixed-effect approaches.
The use of multiple publication-bias assessments is also a strength because no single test can reliably identify selective reporting under all conditions.
This meta-analysis further extends the evidence base beyond the Bösch, Steinkamp, and Boller meta-analysis by incorporating studies published from 2004 through 2026.
The search strategy combined database searching, examination of specialist journals and conference proceedings, AIassisted reference identification, and direct contact with researchers in the field.
This multi-source approach was intended to reduce the likelihood that relevant studies were overlooked.
Several limitations constrain the interpretation of the present findings.
First, the pooled effects are extremely small.

Even where statistically significant, effect sizes of this magnitude are highly vulnerable to minor methodological artifacts, imperfect randomization, data-processing decisions, optional stopping, selective reporting, or unrecognized dependencies among observations.
Statistical significance should therefore not be equated with practical or theoretical significance.
Second, the number of studies available for several analyses was limited, particularly in moderator subgroups.
This reduces statistical power, broadens confidence intervals, and makes estimates of heterogeneity unstable.
The high heterogeneity observed among selected-participant studies further limits confidence in the corresponding subgroup estimate.

Third, the operationalization of effect sizes as the reported statistic divided by the square root of the number of trials assumes comparability across diverse experimental designs and statistical procedures.

Fourth, the operationalization of effect sizes as the reported statistic divided by the square root of the number of trials assumes comparability across diverse experimental designs and statistical procedures.
Differences in RNG hardware, trial definition, aggregation methods, pre-processing, baseline conditions, and inferential tests may affect the comparability of standardized estimates.
Future meta-analyses would benefit from detailed coding of these design features and from sensitivity analyses using alternative effect-size metrics.
Fifth, the indirect or field-based literature presents distinctive challenges.

These studies often rely on naturally occurring events and large-scale datasets, where event inclusion, event timing, timewindow selection, outcome specification, and secondary analyses may be difficult to standardize fully.
Consequently, even a large volume of recorded RNG data cannot compensate for insufficiently constrained hypotheses or post hoc analytic flexibility.
Finally, the present meta-analysis evaluates statistical patterns rather than the underlying mechanism.

The findings cannot distinguish between a genuine mind-matter interaction, methodological artifacts, expectancy effects, selective reporting, statistical misspecification, or alternative theoretical accounts such as decision augmentation.
Stronger evidence will require designs capable of differentiating among these competing explanations.

Future direct-intention studies should use preregistered protocols that specify the primary outcome, direction of the predicted effect, stopping rule, number of trials, exclusion criteria, statistical model, and treatment of missing or corrupted data.
Studies should also employ automated data capture, tamper-evident logs, independent monitoring of RNG performance, and public sharing of raw data and analysis code.
Multi-laboratory collaborations are especially important.
Large, preregistered replication projects using identical hardware and analysis plans could determine whether small effects are reproducible across independent laboratories.
Such studies should include both selected and unselected participants, allowing a prospectively specified test of whether participant characteristics moderate outcomes.
Recruitment, screening, and selection procedures should be reported transparently.
Direct studies should also compare unidirectional and bidirectional intention tasks within the same experimental framework.
This would clarify whether the larger point estimate observed for bidirectional tasks reflects a genuine task-related difference or differences in study design and reporting.
Including sham conditions, blinded experimenters, automated randomization, and negativecontrol analyses would further strengthen causal inference.
For indirect or field-based studies, future protocols should define event-selection criteria, observation windows, primary outcomes, and statistical analyses before events occur whenever possible.
Event registries, timestamped predictions, independent event adjudication, and transparent rules for handling overlapping or unexpected events would reduce concerns about retrospective selection.
Analyses should distinguish clearly between confirmatory tests and exploratory follow-up analyses.
Finally, future meta-analyses should include prospectively registered null studies, and more detailed methodological coding.
Sensitivity analyses for reporting bias, and assessment of study quality could provide a more informative estimate of the evidential value of the literature.
Until such evidence is available, the present findings should be regarded as suggestive but insufficient to establish that human mental intention produces reliable physical deviations in RNG output.
